name: 0G (pre-cellular)
source_1: Rappaport, Wireless Communications: Principles and Practice, 2nd ed., Sec. 1.1
source_2: ITU-R Handbook on Land Mobile (including wireless access), Vol. 1
discrepancy_notes: Section 1.2 lists 0G as a placeholder row without technical parameters; the 0G label is a retrospective category. Cross-checks agree the term is not a standardised ITU designation.
problems_solved: Manual operator assistance per call was slow and unscalable. | No hand-off between base stations - calls dropped on movement. | Capacity limited to a few dozen simultaneous users per city.

name: 1G (analog cellular)
source_1: Rappaport, Sec. 1.2, AMPS voice channel approx. 3 kHz analog
discrepancy_notes: Peak rate is often quoted as 2.4 kbit/s for the digitised voice codec. Field quality depended on analog SNR, not bit rate; the number is a useful summary, not a data service rate.
problems_solved: Incompatible national analog standards (AMPS/NMT/TACS) prevented roaming. | Analog voice was trivial to eavesdrop - no encryption. | Cloned handsets (fraud) were widespread because authentication was trivial. | Capacity per cell was very low and could not scale with demand.

name: 2G (digital cellular)
discrepancy_notes: Section 1.2's 64 kbit/s is theoretical; measured circuit-switched GSM data was 9.6 kbit/s per timeslot. GPRS (2.5G) and EDGE raised typical rates to 40-200 kbit/s but required additional standards beyond the 2G baseline.
problems_solved: 1G fragmentation: GSM unified a common air interface across Europe. | 1G security: GSM introduced authentication and A5 ciphering. | Capacity: TDMA and CDMA supported many more users per cell than FDMA. | Text: SMS created the first mass-market data service.

name: 2.5G (GPRS / EDGE)
discrepancy_notes: Circuit-switched data was inefficient for bursty internet traffic. GPRS introduced packet switching; EDGE improved spectral efficiency 3x.
problems_solved: Circuit-switched data monopolised a channel for the entire session. | No 'always-on' connectivity - every session needed dial-up. | Billing per minute discouraged data usage.

name: 3G (IMT-2000)
discrepancy_notes: Section 1.2's 2 Mbit/s was the ITU IMT-2000 requirement for stationary users. Real deployments delivered 384 kbit/s initially. HSPA (3.5G) later achieved peak rates up to 42 Mbit/s, well beyond the 2 Mbit/s baseline.
problems_solved: 2G data rates were too low for web browsing or video. | No quality-of-service differentiation between voice and data. | Spectral efficiency limits capped capacity under growing demand.

name: 4G (IMT-Advanced)
discrepancy_notes: 100 Mbit/s was the ITU requirement for high-mobility users; 1 Gbit/s for low-mobility. LTE-Advanced Pro (4.5G) reached 1 Gbit/s in the field. Section 1.2's number reflects the 4G baseline, not the eventual cap.
problems_solved: 3G was optimised for voice; data was an afterthought. | Circuit-switched fallback complicated an all-IP core. | MIMO and OFDMA were needed for high spectral efficiency.

name: 5G NR
source_2: 3GPP TS 38.101 (NR UE radio transmission and reception)
discrepancy_notes: 20 Gbit/s is the ITU IMT-2020 peak requirement for eMBB in ideal conditions. Field measurements in 2023-2024 sub-6 deployments report 100-600 Mbit/s downlink typical. mmWave small cells reach multi-Gbit/s but with limited coverage. The gap between peak and typical is the largest of any generation.
problems_solved: 4G could not meet sub-1 ms latency for industrial control. | Massive IoT (10^6 devices/km2) exceeded 4G connection density limits. | Mobile data demand outpaced 4G spectral efficiency improvements.

name: 6G (in research)
source_2: Samsung 6G White Paper, 'The Next Hyper-Connected Experience' (2020)
discrepancy_notes: 1 Tbit/s is a research target, not a standardised requirement. IMT-2030 framework (2023) describes 6G use cases but does not commit to a peak number. Section 1.2's figure is optimistic and should be treated as a research direction, not a validated specification.
problems_solved: 5G's peak-to-typical gap widened; user experience lags headline claims. | AI workloads at the edge need integrated compute and communication. | Sensing and communication convergence not addressed by 5G.
